#9841. Microsoft Links Storm-0940 to ConnectWise Supply Chain Attack

The China-linked actor used an AI-enabled penetration-testing tool to automate and accelerate its attack on more than 2,200 tenants.

A China-linked threat actor that Microsoft tracks as Storm-0940 used an agentic AI penetration-testing framework to accelerate a supply chain attack involving ConnectWise Cloud Backup.

The attackers used compromised application credentials associated with the service to attempt to access the Microsoft 365 environments of more than 2,250 downstream customer tenants. In multiple instances, the attackers obtained privileged access to an organization’s cloud infrastructure in less than three hours after initial targeting, Microsoft said in an analysis published this week.

The activity demonstrates how threat actors are integrating agentic AI into existing offensive security workflows and scaling their operations exponentially, Microsoft researchers wrote. "While the majority of the targeting wasn't successful, Storm-0940 achieved privileged cloud persistence at many organizations in a brief time," they said.

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

ConnectWise provides software and IT management technology that managed service providers use to deliver a broad range of services to their customers, including backup and recovery for Microsoft 365 data. Delivering these services requires the company to have authorized application access to customer Microsoft 365 environments to back up and restore data.

On Oct. 16, ConnectWise disclosed unauthorized access to application identities associated with its Cloud Backup product. The company subsequently published additional details and containment guidance but has not publicly explained how the attackers initially gained control of the application identities.

Microsoft described the incident as part of a broader Storm-0940 campaign that began as early as September and targeted hundreds of organizations worldwide across several industries including manufacturing, aerospace, chemicals, energy, defense, and financial services. The threat actor has been using an AI penetration-testing framework called ARTEX to automate and accelerate its operations.

"In multiple affected environments, Microsoft observed AI-accelerated follow-on activity through Microsoft Graph, including reconnaissance, application credential changes, and attempts to modify privileges that could enable expanded or persistent access," Microsoft said.

In the ConnectWise incident, Storm-0940 used ARTEX to accelerate reconnaissance and scanning, password spraying, and OAuth application abuse. The threat actor used ARTEX to attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants, generating as many as 2,900 sign-in attempts per minute. That pace left defenders with little time to detect and respond to the activity, Microsoft noted.

Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

"Storm-0940's activity illustrates how a threat actor with a broad target set can use an agentic AI tool and privileged authentication material to quickly attempt to compromise many organizations," the company said.

ConnectWise suspended its Cloud Backup service and also took its SaaS Security and Cloud Management services offline following the incident. In an Oct. 22 update, the company noted it was continuing work on restoring disrupted services and urged customers to keep affected ConnectWise application connections offline until further notice.

"Investigation and monitoring continue alongside restoration. Existing backup archives remain encrypted, isolated and preserved, with no indication of compromise," the company said. ConnectWise called on customers to review their individual Microsoft 365 environments using the company's technical investigation and remediation guide and related information.

Microsoft meanwhile highlighted its own mitigation and protection guidance, which included recommendations like reviewing every Microsoft 365 tenant that might have been tied to ConnectWise and to preserve logs and other forensic evidence before making any changes.

Related:Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

Ross Filipek, CISO at Corsica Technologies, says that before reconnecting with ConnectWise, affected organizations should have a clear understanding of what might have happened inside their environment. He pointed to Microsoft's discovery of application credential changes that could give attackers a way back in to compromised environments. Organizations are going to need to investigate whether their Microsoft 365 environments are safe before they reconnect, he says.

"Keep affected connections disabled in line with vendor guidance. Investigate unauthorized changes that could leave another way in. Preserve evidence without delaying containment," Filipek tells Dark Reading. "There's also an immediate business question: Are backups still running? Assign someone on each side to check coverage during the interruption. A restored connection needs verification that backup jobs are completing and recovery works."

Going forward, organizations need to have a recovery plan that takes into account the potential of their losing access to a service that they normally would depend on for recovery, Filipek adds. Incident responders should know which applications connect to the organization's Microsoft 365 tenant and how to quickly sever those connections when necessary, and exercise that scenario with their service provider.

"Establish who checks backup coverage during containment and who decides whether the business can tolerate the interruption. Leaving those responsibilities implied is how both sides end up assuming the other has checked," he says.

Jon Baker, vice president of threat-informed defense at AttackIQ, wants affected organizations to preserve sign-in and audit records and to investigate application sign-ins, Microsoft Graph activity, new credentials, privilege changes, and unusual data access. "Remove confirmed unauthorized access and verify vendor and tenant remediation separately," he advises. "After containment, controlled validation can test whether comparable application behavior can still reach sensitive resources or establish another foothold."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9840. NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders. Unlike many generative visual language models, NeoMME does not use a separate pretrained vision tower or a causal language model. A single bidirectional Transformer processes both text tokens and raw image patches, and we train the entire model from scratch with a masked discrete-diffusion objective.

We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach. NeoMME-Retriever returns dense and late-interaction embeddings in one forward pass. Both model sizes lie on the ViDoRe v3 Pareto frontier for nDCG@10 and model size. At a matched 2048×2048 image input size on an NVIDIA L40S GPU, the 260M model encodes about 51 pages per second, or about twice ColModernVBERT's throughput. Hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization reduce late-interaction index storage from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page (255× smaller) while retaining more than 95% of baseline nDCG@10.

NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers. We release all model checkpoints under the Apache 2.0 license.

Many recent visual document retrievers are adapted from pretrained generative visual language models. A separately pretrained vision encoder produces visual features, which a projector maps into the language model's input space. A causal decoder then processes the combined image and text representations. Retrieval, classification, and token labeling do not generate text autoregressively, so they do not require a causal decoder or the parameter and compute overhead of this architecture.

ModernBERT brought efficient architecture and training improvements to bidirectional encoders. For visual document retrieval, ModernVBERT applied a bidirectional ModernBERT-style text encoder while retaining a separate pretrained SigLIP2 vision tower. We wanted to push this even further by designing and training a multimodal encoder without having to carry over the parameter and compute overhead of a VLM.

NeoMME (pronounced "nee-oh-me", IPA /ˈniː.oʊ.mi/) is a multilingual, multimodal foundation encoder that generates vector representations for input text and/or images using a single Transformer encoder. It is not based on an existing pretrained vision tower, text encoder, or text decoder.

Images and text use the same computational path, so NeoMME can more easily support pretraining, fine-tuning, parallelization, and serving across both modalities.

NeoMME comes in two sizes, 260M and 800M. Both variants share the same architecture:

We pretrain NeoMME from scratch as a discrete masked-diffusion text denoiser. For each text-only example, we sample a corruption rate uniformly between 0 and 1. Each eligible text token is then independently masked at that rate.

Multimodal examples use corruption rates between 0.3 and 1. The image patches remain visible while NeoMME reconstructs masked text. With light masking, the model can often recover a missing word from the surrounding text alone. For example, "cat" is a plausible completion of "The [MASK] sat on the mat," even without an image. But high masking forces the model to learn image-grounded descriptions with little to no signal from the non-masked input text tokens.

Pretraining mixes multilingual text, code, mathematics, natural images, and document images. Each model processes about 524 billion packed input tokens, including 290 billion tokens from text-only examples. This text budget is relatively small compared with ModernBERT's 2 trillion training token budget. Hence, we chose the NorMuon optimizer to improve data efficiency during training.

To get a meaningful downstream evaluation of the backbone, we fine-tune NeoMME for visual document retrieval using the page-image methodology introduced by ColPali. While traditional text-based retrieval consists of retrieving text chunks, NeoMME-Retriever ranks document page screenshots and bypasses all the preprocessing OCR steps necessary to extract text from PDFs. Treating the pages as images preserves layout, charts, tables, font type and size, and other visual clues that cannot be captured even by a perfect OCR model.

NeoMME-Retriever reuses the NeoMME backbone but adds two jointly trained heads on top of it for retrieval:

Omar Khattab, who introduced late-interaction in ColBERT, explains why the term is more precise than "multi-vector." It describes the granularity and learnability of the scoring function, not simply the number of stored vectors.

To learn more about late-interaction, we recommend reading this crash course by Amélie Chatelain.

One NeoMME-Retriever forward pass returns both representations, which gives you flexibility no matter your use case and infrastructure. We recommend using late-interaction embeddings in general since they are more powerful and can be used easily with open-source libraries like NextPlaid. However, if you have a very large corpora, you can run a single forward pass with NeoMME-Retriever to get the dense embedding, retrieve a small number of documents through an ANN index, and then use late-interaction to rerank the retrieved candidates.

We report nDCG@10 on ViDoRe v3. NeoMME-Retriever-260M reaches 0.523, the highest score among evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters. It is within 0.002 nDCG@10 of ColQwen2.5 while using about 14× fewer parameters. NeoMME-Retriever-800M reaches 0.556, within 0.009 nDCG@10 of the similarly sized Vultron Retriever Flash (0.8B). Both NeoMME-Retriever models lie on the model-size Pareto frontier.

ViDoRe v1 and v2 use nDCG@5. On both benchmarks, NeoMME-Retriever-260M outperforms ColModernVBERT and the twice-larger ColSmol-500M. NeoMME-Retriever-800M outperforms ColPali v1.3 while using 3.6 times fewer parameters.

† Scores from MTEB. ‡ Results from our own evaluations.

Late-interaction storage scales linearly with the number of vectors in the output embedding. Higher-resolution images contain more patches, so they produce larger embeddings. For example, a 2048×2048 square page produces embeddings containing 4,200 vectors with NeoMME-Retriever, or about 2.1 MB in float32. Across the ViDoRe v3 benchmark, the measured average is about 1.5 MB per document.

To reduce the storage footprint of the late-interaction index, we combine two complementary compression methods:

We tested this setup on ViDoRe v3. With a pooling factor 10 and int8 queries and documents, storage decreased from about 1.5 MB to 39 kB per page, a 39× reduction, while keeping more than 99% of the baseline nDCG@10. A more aggressive configuration uses pooling factor 8, int8 queries, and binary documents. That version uses 6 kB per page (255× smaller) and keeps more than 95% of the original retrieval quality.

Users can pick a compression setting from that frontier based on storage budget and required retrieval quality.

Before you can search a corpus, a retriever model must turn your documents into embeddings, which will be stored in a vector store like Qdrant, Weaviate, or Milvus. Faster encoding makes building and adding new documents to the index faster, thus reducing the GPU uptime and compute cost required.

So we measured image encoding speeds for NeoMME-Retriever against other multimodal document retrievers. We used preprocessed image tensors and calibrated the batch size separately for each model and image size. At a matched 2048×2048 input size on one NVIDIA L40S, NeoMME-Retriever-260M encodes about 51 pages per second, nearly twice ColModernVBERT's 26 pages per second. Both 260M and 800M NeoMME-Retriever models are also faster than the other models we compared on smaller input images.

NeoMME-Retriever (260M and 800M) returns dense and multi-vector embeddings together. The example below scores two text queries against two document-page images with MeanMaxSim late interaction and dense cosine similarity.

We provide separate dense and late-interaction checkpoints for fine-tuning with Sentence Transformers v6. Following the same pattern as text encoders such as ModernBERT, Sentence Transformers loads the backbone through NeoMMEModel rather than the dual-head NeoMMEForRetrieval class. Sentence Transformers currently supports one retrieval head per model, so each checkpoint lets you fine-tune the dense or late-interaction head independently. To train both heads together, use NeoMMEForRetrieval with a custom Trainer.

Visual document retrieval can be used as the first stage of a visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Unlike text RAG, which retrieves extracted text chunks, visual RAG retrieves the original page images and sends them to a visual language model. The model can then use tables, plots, diagrams, and page layout that text extraction may flatten or omit. Here is how visual RAG works:

You can test visual RAG directly with NeoMME-Retriever in our HF Space: 🤗 tonywu71/neomme-retriever-demo.

NeoMME replaces separate pretrained image and text encoders with one long-context bidirectional Transformer. We train it from scratch to process both multilingual text tokens and raw 32×32 image patches.

NeoMME-Retriever is a fine-tuned version of NeoMME for visual document retrieval. One forward pass produces both dense and late-interaction representations. The 260M model outperforms all evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters and, at a matched 2048×2048 input size, encodes pages at about 2× ColModernVBERT's throughput. To reduce the large storage footprint of late-interaction embeddings for high-resolution documents, we experimented with hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization and managed to reduce the late-interaction embeddings from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page, a 255× compression, while retaining more than 95% of the baseline nDCG@10.

We release all NeoMME model checkpoints and a day-zero Hugging Face Transformers implementation to allow practitioners to build efficient multimodal and multilingual representation models on top of our work.

NeoMME began as a side quest between two good friends. We worked with limited time and compute, and we decided to share the results so the community can build on them. We thank H Company for supporting the work and providing the compute used to train NeoMME.

#9839. State Bank of India Suffers a Customer PII Data Leak

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Relatively small data breaches in India can turn quite serious, thanks to a sophisticated underground market for trading PII.

An anonymous hacker has leaked a small batch of sensitive customer records from the State Bank of India (SBI), with potentially serious consequences for the thousands impacted.

SBI has been posting a lot about cybersecurity on social media lately. In August it introduced a new CGI mascot named "Captain Y." Captain Y from SBI is "your Cyber Protector," he says in his promo video, "with awareness as his superpower." SBI's best plug for cybersecurity awareness came on Wednesday, though, when it publicly disclosed that it had suffered a breach of customer data.

In a notice to India's National Stock Exchange, the organization's compliance and company secretary acknowledged that 3,897 customer records had been leaked online. They did not specify whether those records belonged to 3,897 individual customers. In a public notice to customers, the state-run bank emphasized that the incident really only impacted "a very, very small number of customers."

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

For a bank that serves north of 500 million people, a few thousand records does indeed qualify as very, very small. Cyber experts note, though, that for those affected, the consequences could be significant thanks to India's sophisticated underground economy for buying and selling personally identifying information (PII).

Last week, a new account with the name "Siriusim" published a post to the mainstream data breach website BreachForums. They had new user data from SBI, they claimed, including personal user information, new account and loan applications, and more. The data included a table with 375,000 rows, and 2,722 PDF files. Importantly, neither figure necessarily indicated the total number of individuals impacted.

As part of the post, Siriusim featured a few documents with handwritten personal information. Mumbai's Free Press Journal verified that PII from the breach samples was valid, belonging to real Indian citizens. One individual, for example, lost their mobile number and know your customer (KYC) documentation in the breach, and the WhatsApp photograph associated with their number matched the passport photo included in the KYC file.

SBI acknowledged that leaked data included names, genders, mobile numbers, email addresses, home addresses, dates of birth, bank profile IDs, metadata associated with loans, and "other files." Follow-on reporting out of Mumbai suggested that this extra data included Central KYC numbers — a single identifier for financial accounts in India — and video KYC verification data, and the kinds of files one might have to submit in the process of creating a new bank account, or filing for a loan. For instance, one published document included an individual's employment and income declaration, with details about their current employer, work experience, and salary.

Related:Russian Influence Operation Widely Targets Latin America

Exactly what precipitated the leak, and why it affected only 0.0008% of the bank's customers, remains unclear. In its formal declaration, SBI emphasized that "the bank's core business functions continue to operate normally without disruptions." Altogether, these clues might point to a breach of some peripheral digital service or data-handling system, rather than the core bank system.

In fact, SBI's last major customer data leak followed just such a script. In 2019, it exposed customer account data through a single server at a Mumbai data center, which was missing password protection. The server supported its "SBI Quick" system, used to text and call customers about basic account information. That one machine put millions of customers at risk, perhaps highlighting just how minor this new leak really is.

"If the data is genuine, the main risk is not direct account theft but credible-sounding phishing, vishing, and identity or loan fraud, since attackers who know someone’s details can impersonate the bank convincingly," explains independent security researcher Sushant Bhardwaj.

Related:Venezuelan Cartel's Malware Honcho Nabbed for ATM Jackpotting

Email addresses, phone numbers, and dates of birth carry fairly obvious risk in the hands of bad actors, and less common kinds of PII can add color to otherwise generic identity attacks. For instance, "KYC details are hard to change, so they can support identity fraud, such as applying for credit in someone else’s name or answering account-verification questions," Bhardwaj notes. And with regard to loan metadata, "a caller who can quote real loan details can pose as the bank or a recovery agent and pressure a borrower into paying a 'fee' or sharing a one-time password (OTP)."

Brian Hussey, senior vice president for Cyderes' Howler Cell, goes deeper. Last month, his team reported on an Indian data broker selling personal records for only about 5 rupees (6 cents or so) per lookup, through a Telegram bot and business application programming interface (API) platform. Using these simple lookups, cybercriminals targeting Indian citizens can obtain vast stores of PII belonging to regular citizens in an instant. And data breaches like SBI's, Hussey notes, can feed into this underground economy. "A breach dump goes stale the day it's posted. A live lookup service is always current, because it is asking the authoritative source in real time. India’s underground data market has both, and they work together," he explains.

"India built one of the most connected identity systems in the world, and an entire industry exists to query it," he warns. "That connectivity is what makes a leak in one place so impactful and useful somewhere else."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9838. A Look at Datastar

I have always been interested in frontend solutions for building web applications. Even though I’m more of a backend programmer, I really dig all the different techniques people come up with for creating browser-based apps that are both reactive (reflecting remote state in real-time) and interactive (responding to user actions).

Over the last few years, I’ve been looking at different frontend frameworks and libraries, to see how they work, and what I can learn from them. I adore Svelte, which is really smart and efficient. Its sister framework SvelteKit inspired the file-based routing in my own web framework for Ruby, Syntropy. I also really like the approach of the Phoenix framework to building reactive apps using LiveView, which is an amazing technology that builds on the solid concurrency foundation of Elixir/Erlang.

Many people have tried to recreate the same functionality for other languages or frameworks, with varying degrees of success. Recently, Marco Roth came up with ReActionView, which promises to bring reactive views to Rails apps, building on his previous work on Herb, a set of tools that improve on the developer experience of writing ERB templates for Rails apps.

All those different technologies are certainly impressive, but they all are tied to specific languages/frameworks: Svelte/SvelteKit is a JS framework, LiveView is for Phoenix/Elixir, ReActionView is for Ruby on Rails, LiveWire is for Laravel/PHP, etc.

And then there’s Datastar, which dubs itself “the Hypermedia framework”. It is somewhat similar to other frontend declarative frameworks/libraries such as HTMX or Alpine.js, in that interactivity/reactivity is done declaratively by adding attributes to HTML tags. But what is different about Datastar is that it insists on keeping state where it should be, such that it doesn’t try to copy server state to the client and keep it in sync with the server. Instead, the server continuously sends updates (in the form of HTML patches, or signal patches) to the client. In that respect, Datastar is more like LiveView, but without the coupling to Phoenix/Elixir. In fact, Datastar offers SDKs for different languages and frameworks, including Ruby (the Ruby SDK is maintained by Ismael Celis).

I find this approach so refereshing! With Datastar, you can use any backend technology in order to build reactive web apps. Furthermore, Datastar relies on SSE (server-sent events) for streaming updates from the server to the client, instead of the somewhat older approach of using a WebSocket connection used in technologies such as LiveView, or HotWire (the current go-to solution for Rails apps).

While SSE does not provide a full-duplex connection to the server (meaning, you can’t use an SSE request/connection to send data from the client to the server), it provides two important advantages over WebSocket: A WebSocket connection normally requires establishing a separate HTTP/1.1 connection to the server (there’s partial support for WebSocket over HTTP/2, but that depends on the browser and the server/reverse proxy used. HTTP/3 support is very limited as far as I could tell). In contrast, SSE requests can be multiplexed on top of an HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 connection, along with any number of other concurrent requests. Secondly, because SSE requests are just normal (streaming) HTTP requests, the server can use standard HTTP compression in order to achieve significant reduction in bandwidth.

Let’s look at a simple example of working with Datastar. Here’s the markup for a simple reactive app that displays the current time on the server:

This example does three things: load the datastar library (BTW it’s only about 15KB!), set up a connection to an SSE stream at /ds/time_stream using the @get action, and binds a span to a signal named $time. On the server side, the controller looks as follows (using Syntropy):

The controller code is quite simple: after calling respond_sse, which sends some HTTP response headers, we send a first update, then we send further updates once per second. What actually gets sent over the wire looks as follows:

The Datastar wire protocol is based on the SSE response format, where each event contains an (optional) event: entry and one or more data: entries. Distinct events are separated by double newline characters (\n\n). In this case, we’re sending a datastar-patch-signals event that tells the browser to update signal values. The patched values are expressed as a JSON object where the keys correspond to signal names and the values correspond to the signal values.

You can look at this example on a separate page, but for the sake of convenience I’ll go ahead and embed it right here:

Although this is a very simple example, look at all the things we’re not doing 😜: we don’t need to set up an EventSource object, or use fetch to start the SSE connection on the client side, we don’t need to go through the DOM and update anything that’s bound to the $time signal. On the server side we just stream changes to the server state to the client (eventually though, we might want to introduce some abstractions for sending a datastar-patch-signals event or other types of events, but this is pretty trivial…)

Let’s look at how signals are handled in Datastar a bit more closely. I’ve been playing with Datastar in the last few days and have observed the some peculiarities:

In Datastar, signals are global to the page. They can’t be scoped to a part of the DOM, but they can be namespaced by nesting them inside objects:

Alternatively, you can use the following notation, handy when you have key values that contain slashes, or other special characters:

By default, Datastar will send all signal values back to the server on every user action, which may be problematic if you have lots of signals on your page. In order to prevent signal values from being sent to the server on each request, the signal name must begin with an underscore.

Finally, an important aspect of Datastar signals (and indeed, Datastar in general,) is that Datastar doesn’t really have a Javascript API. You can’t just access signal values from Javascript (this is by design), which may make it harder to integrate Datastar with other tools. But there is a workaround for that and it’s pretty simple:

InfoQ Homepage News LinkedIn Uses OpenTelemetry to Trace the Member Journey from Tap to Backend

Nov 03, 2026 3 min read

LinkedIn has built an OpenTelemetry-based telemetry platform that connects what members do in its iOS, Android, and web applications with the backend services processing those interactions.

The goal is to close a common observability gap. Client analytics can show that a member tapped a button or encountered an error, while backend tracing explains what happened inside the services handling the request. Historically, connecting these views required engineers to correlate separate systems. LinkedIn's approach allows a member interaction to be followed from the client through frontend and backend services to the underlying data stores.

A single page can generate numerous requests, each potentially passing through multiple services. LinkedIn introduced a pageForestId to provide context above individual distributed traces.

Each request retains its OpenTelemetry traceId, while related requests from the same page context can be associated through the pageForestId. Engineers can therefore investigate both an individual request and the wider activity that contributed to a member's experience.

This is important because conventional distributed tracing generally follows one request, whereas a member journey can involve many related requests.

LinkedIn operates a diverse technology stack spanning mobile and web clients alongside backend services written in Java, Python, Go, and Rust. OpenTelemetry provides a common model for instrumentation, trace context, and semantic conventions across those environments.

LinkedIn has built its own wrappers and extensions around the standard OpenTelemetry SDKs, allowing product teams to use consistent instrumentation while the platform handles concerns such as mobile lifecycle, export, and LinkedIn-specific metadata.

Client and backend applications generate OpenTelemetry spans, with trace context propagated as requests move through the system. Shared HTTP and gRPC frameworks automatically instrument common request paths, while teams can add explicit spans around important business operations.

Telemetry is transported through Apache Kafka and stored in ClickHouse, with pageForestId, traceId, and timestamps providing the keys for correlation. This allows engineers to begin with a member-facing interaction and drill into the backend execution responsible for it.

Capturing every span would generate an enormous amount of telemetry, making sampling fundamental to the architecture.

LinkedIn uses coordinated head sampling so related client and server activity receives a consistent sampling decision. A pseudonymised member identifier helps maintain that consistency across the journey, preventing the client from being sampled while the corresponding backend trace is discarded, or vice versa.

The company also distinguishes valuable quality-of-experience telemetry from lower-value debugging information. LinkedIn estimates that up to 90% of some backend tracing volume could potentially be treated as debug-level data.

Client-side observability introduces additional constraints. Mobile applications can be suspended or terminated before telemetry is transmitted, so LinkedIn batches spans but can flush telemetry when an application moves into the background.

The platform also applies controls around what data can enter traces, including attribute allowlists, denylists, and redaction. This is important because distributed traces can otherwise become an unintended channel for sensitive application or member information.

Traditional distributed tracing tools such as Jaeger and Grafana Tempo are primarily focused on following requests across backend services. Commercial platforms such as Datadog and New Relic also combine distributed tracing with real-user and application monitoring.

LinkedIn's approach is less about introducing a capability that these platforms cannot provide and more about making OpenTelemetry the common foundation connecting its client and backend telemetry. Its own pageForestId model adds a higher-level grouping around standard traces, while Kafka and ClickHouse provide a customised ingestion and storage architecture.

This also gives LinkedIn greater control over its observability stack and avoids making application instrumentation dependent on a particular commercial backend.

A member does not experience a traceId; they experience a page that loads slowly, an action that fails, or a feature that behaves unexpectedly. Connecting those experiences to the distributed systems behind them gives engineers a much more direct path from user impact to technical cause.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog

#9836. Fedora Linux 45 released

Fedora Linux 45 has been released. This includes all editions: Fedora Workstation, Fedora KDE Plasma Desktop, Fedora Server, Fedora Cloud, Fedora CoreOS, and Fedora IoT, as well as the Atomic Desktops and Spins.

This release adds support for installation on Stratis storage using Anaconda or Kickstart installs, retires unmaintained VPN plugins for NetworkManager, and updates Fedora's desktop environments, developer toolchains, and system packages. See the Fedora wiki ChangeSet page for a list of major changes.

#9835. Rebuilding AUTOMATIC1111 with Gradio Workflow

In our last post, we built five small gr.Workflow graphs and hinted at what it would take to build something as complex as AUTOMATIC1111's stable-diffusion-webui. In this post we walk you through Workflow1111, where we have rebuilt most of AUTOMATIC1111's feature set as a single workflow canvas.

Workflow1111 is a graph of eleven media pipelines built using seventy-three nodes. It brings together SOTA models for text-to-image, hi-resolution fix, image-to-image, prompt-matrix grids, VLM interrogate, detection-to-inpaint masks, ControlNet-style annotators, background removal, PNG Info storing, and image-to-video.

You can run any of these pipelines by signing in with your Hugging Face account or providing an access token. Once you sign in, the model calls use your own quota.

👉 Try Workflow1111, or duplicate the Space and start rewiring it for your own use case.

All the media pipelines are built from the same four operator kinds covered in our last post and the official guide. Each node on the canvas wraps one operator, and the operator's inputs and outputs become the ports you connect edges to. As a quick reference on our four operator kinds: fn is a Python function, model is a model called through InferenceClient, space is another Gradio Space, and dataset is a row from a Hub dataset.

Let's go through the pipelines one by one.

This is the core pipeline. It has the controls you'd expect from A1111's txt2img tab: negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, width and height, plus a model_id field for choosing the checkpoint. The prompt goes through a prompt-builder fn node first, which appends the selected style preset and cleans up the text, then into a model node that calls the checkpoint through Inference Providers. A post-process fn node writes the generation parameters into the PNG's metadata on the way out, which is what the PNG Info pipeline reads back later.

In Automatic1111, hi-resolution fix first upscales the txt2img output and then runs a second denoising pass. Here it's a two-node detour instead. The text-to-image result goes into a FLUX.1-Kontext model node with a refine instruction ("enhance fine detail and micro-texture, keep the composition identical") and comes back sharper and larger.

That same Kontext node doubles as the image-to-image tab. Upload an image, describe the change you want, and it returns the edited image.

Start with a rough prompt like "A lighthouse in a storm." This pipeline sends it to a Qwen3-4B model node, and a small fn node turns the reply into a clean list of tags, capped at forty: "stormy sea, wet rocks, dramatic composition, low angle shot, volumetric lighting, ominous tone." You can connect any diffusion model node to this output to render the image.

There's no custom node involved, unlike in ComfyUI. In a Gradio workflow the LLM and the diffusion model are both ordinary model operators on the same canvas.

This is like AUTOMATIC1111's Interrogate button, with a VLM doing the interrogating instead of CLIP. Qwen2.5-VL looks at a night-market photo and writes a prompt that could have produced it. A ViT classifier node reads the same image and returns labels: restaurant 51.9%, tobacco shop 15.6%, toyshop 9.1%.

Both nodes use the same image input, so gr.Workflow runs them in parallel and you get both answers in roughly the time it takes to run one.

AUTOMATIC1111 makes you paint an inpaint mask by hand. This pipeline generates one from a detector instead. DETR finds six objects in a street photo (three people, a dog, a bicycle, and a car), and from there the workflow splits into two branches: one draws the detected boxes on the original image, the other turns them into a mask you can feed into an inpaint pipeline downstream.

The drawing and the mask creation both happen locally with Pillow and NumPy. Only the detection call leaves the machine.

This is like AUTOMATIC1111's prompt matrix. A base prompt, "a lone oak tree," gets combined with four suffixes (at sunrise, in a thunderstorm, under the Milky Way, in autumn fog) by a fn node, and each variant goes to its own text-to-image node. A final node stitches the four results into one contact sheet.

gr.Workflow has no loop operator, so the four text-to-image nodes sit side by side on the canvas. Since they're at the same dependency depth they run in parallel, and all four images start generating at once.

This is like the Extras tab in Automatic1111. There are two upscaler nodes, and they take different routes. The first is a local Lanczos resample in an fn node, which needs no network call and finishes as fast as Pillow can resize. The second is AuraSR ×4, and it's the first space node on the canvas: it calls a Space on the Hub and treats the result like any other node output.

Background removal works the same way. BRIA RMBG-2.0 is another space node, so the whole model lives in its own Space and this canvas just calls it in.

Canny, line art, sketch, luma-depth, and posterize are the preprocessors you'd normally get from the ControlNet extension in Automatic1111. Here, each one is a fn node written in plain NumPy, with no model behind it. On a pre-loaded example photo of a building facade, each annotator takes about half a second on CPU.

There are 36 operator nodes in the app, 32 are fn nodes, and 22 of those run entirely in-process without a network call. Roughly two-thirds of the canvas keeps working if you lose your connection. Since these are regular Python functions, you can also test them directly, with no canvas, server, or GPU involved.

AUTOMATIC1111 stores generation details in the PNG's parameters text chunk, and the PNG Info tab reads them back. Workflow1111 does the same. The post-process node on the text-to-image pipeline writes the metadata, and this pipeline reads it back out, including the prompt, negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, image size, and model.

The image node that PNG Info reads from also feeds a Wan 2.2 I2V A14B node, which animates it; in the demo example a sleeping fox wakes up and starts moving. There's no second upload box because one reference node can feed as many downstream pipelines as you need, so a single upload gets its metadata read and gets animated on the same canvas.

So far every model call has gone to someone else's hardware, through Inference Providers or a Space. That's why you can build and run something like Workflow1111 without a GPU of your own.

A fn node is just Python, though, so it can equally load a model locally and run it on your own GPU. FastVideo/fastvideo-fasth3-preview is a gr.Workflow app that does exactly that. It runs FastH3, a four-step distillation of MiniMax-H3, and generates video with a soundtrack on ZeroGPU.

The whole app comes down to one bound function:

ZeroGPU gives the function a GPU when it needs one, then releases it when the call is done. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know about any of that. It just calls the fn node.

This isn't specific to Spaces either. Point bind= to a function that loads a local checkpoint, run .launch() on your own machine, and the Workflow1111 canvas can drive your own GPU.

Every output node on the canvas becomes a REST endpoint, with no routes written by hand. Workflow1111 exposes nine of them: /image, /edited_image, /generated_prompt, /recovered_prompt, /detected_objects, /x_y_grid, /upscaled_local, /annotator_map, and /png_info.

The same endpoints are also MCP tools. Launch with mcp_server=True (guide) and every output node shows up as a tool an AI assistant can call. Point Claude Code, Cursor, or any MCP client at the server URL:

Now an agent can generate an image, read a prompt back out, or run detection as steps in a larger task, with no glue code. Each caller sends their own token in the X-HF-Token header, so the Space holds none of its own.

AUTOMATIC1111 gave us the feature list, but the tool Gradio Workflow really gets compared to is ComfyUI, since both are node graphs. For a lot of what people want to build and ship, gr.Workflow covers the same ground.

The result is a multi-model pipeline that people can open in a browser, sign into, use right away, and call from code.

Workflow1111 has 73 nodes, but it started with just this:

bind= turns your functions into nodes, edges= connects them, and .launch() opens the canvas in your browser so you can keep editing there. When it's ready, gradio deploy puts the whole thing on a Space. The gr.Workflow guide has the full details, including the JSON schema and every operator type.

If you'd rather start from something that already works, open Workflow1111, hit Duplicate, and pick one of the eleven pipelines to change: delete nodes, swap models, rewire the flow. If you'd rather start smaller, the previous post has five workflows you can get running in about a minute each.

Whatever you build, post it on X and tag @gradio. We'd be happy to amplify your workflows.

4-step MiniMax-H3 — video with a matching soundtrack

Automatic1111-style studio on one gr.Workflow canvas

Really impressive breakdown the part that stands out most is how the graph structure gives you free parallelism (the prompt-matrix and interrogate examples) without any extra orchestration code. The mix of fn, model, and space node types on one canvas also makes the ComfyUI comparison land well: you get custom-node flexibility from plain Python, but zero-code REST/MCP endpoints for free. Curious how complex a canvas can get before performance or maintainability becomes a concern has anyone pushed past 73 nodes

Analisis yang sangat mengesankan, bagian yang paling menonjol adalah bagaimana struktur graf memberikan paralelisme gratis (contoh prompt-matrix dan interrogate) tanpa kode orkestrasi tambahan. Perpaduan tipe node fn, model, dan space pada satu kanvas juga membuat perbandingan dengan ComfyUI tepat: Anda mendapatkan fleksibilitas node kustom dari Python biasa, tetapi endpoint REST/MCP tanpa kode secara gratis. Saya penasaran seberapa kompleks sebuah kanvas dapat dibuat sebelum kinerja atau pemeliharaan menjadi masalah, apakah ada yang pernah melampaui 73 node?

#9834. AI Agents as Insider Threats: Inside Microsoft's Bet on a Unified Security Stack

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

Microsoft's Project Perception adds Guardian Agents to monitor and contain anomalous AI agents, but experts warn that policing unpredictable agents with other agents may compound — not contain — the risk.

Microsoft wants security teams to treat artificial intelligence (AI) agents like they treat employees with privileged access: insiders who can make mistakes, be manipulated, or be compromised.

Earlier this week, the software giant introduced new capabilities to Project Perception, enabling it to discover agents running within an organization, assign an identity and permissions to each agent, and continuously score each organization's risk. When an anomalous agent is discovered in the organization's environment — a problem that Microsoft describes as the "agentic insider" — Project Perception can now cut off the agent's access.

The first release of Project Perception, made available in public preview through Microsoft Defender in August, was designed to defend against AI-driven attacks. Focused on Microsoft's security operations center threat and investigation scenarios, it coordinates red agents to scan for attacker paths, blue agents to identify the greatest risks, and green agents to mitigate threats. Project Perception's initial use was vulnerability management, through MDASH, Microsoft's AI code scanner, which is still in preview. MDASH uses several AI models, including MAI-Cyber-1-Flash, the company's first cybersecurity-specialized model.

Related:Investors Dish on New Startups & What They'd Back Next

"We're expanding Perception so that we can go secure the AI insider," said Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security, in a brief video accompanying the announcement.

To do that, Microsoft is adding what it calls Guardian Agents, which monitor the AI-based agents running across an organization and can contain them when they stray into unexpected behavior.

Today, many agents run with the permissions of the user who launched them or by invoking the user's credentials. Microsoft's approach separates the two, Microsoft said in a blog post detailing the new capabilities.

Nadim Abdo, corporate vice president for identity and network access, tells Dark Reading that the system gives every agent a distinct identity separate from the user's "and will ensure that the agent starts with no permissions at all, and only up-scopes to the permissions it needs to complete the task the user is asking it to do,"

Specifically, Microsoft said the new release can detect 35 more types of agents running locally on devices, bringing the total to 60, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot. It also includes:

Extensions to Microsoft Entra Agent ID that can assign an identity to an agent that was never built to work with Entra.

Dynamic Agent Risk, a continuously updated score built from Entra, Defender, Intune, Purview, Sentinel, and signals from Global Secure Access, Microsoft’s security service edge (SSE) solution that unifies network access and identity protection.

Dynamic Conditional Access for agents, which can block writes while keeping reads, restrict network paths, revoke access, or stop an agent's runtime as risk rises.

Microsoft Execution Container (MXC), a sandbox that keeps credentials and security controls outside the agent's reach.

Related:RemoteThreat Bets Security Teams Need to Test What Happens After Defenses Fail

With Project Perception, Abdo describes an expense-approval agent that reads a malicious instruction hidden in an expense report.

"If someone got a prompt that convinced it to start to try to do wire transfers, we can actually watch it accessing a wire transfer system and say, 'Wait a second, that has nothing to do with the intent,' and that raises its risk," he says.

Microsoft says it can act on rising risk immediately, interrupting an agent's live session, network connection, or runtime without disrupting the user's own work, though those are vendor-stated capabilities in preview.

Project Perception has an expanded agent registry that now shows up across the Microsoft 365 admin center, Defender, Entra, Intune, Purview, and a new Perception Agent Insights view. And Dynamic Agent Risk replaces previously siloed risk scores.

Related:Deception by Design: CISA's Guide to Tricking Cybercriminals

The controls themselves sit outside the agents they watch.

"The first thing [an attacker will] do is they'll manipulate the security controls," Abdo says, so the credentials and monitoring tools run outside the container.

Perception and Agent 365, Microsoft's control plane for governing that was introduced last year and made generally available since May, "need to be battle tested," acknowledged Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella during a fireside chat with Gallot during a CISO conference last week at Microsoft's Redmond, Wash., headquarters. He also admitted that Microsoft's own detection must improve.

"If I look at the state of the art of behavioral monitoring of, let's say, Defender, it has to go way up," he said.

Gallot framed the risk in terms of how models behave.

"Those models have proven to be unpredictable," she said. "They'll do anything they can to get from point A to point B, and what they do may not be what you intend them to do."

Much of what Microsoft describes echoes what other vendors announced in recent weeks. Okta's Agent Gateway separates an agent's permissions from those of the user directing it, and Okta plans a kill switch that would reject tokens already issued to a deactivated agent. Teleport, backed by Cisco, ties privileges to tasks so they disappear when the work ends. CrowdStrike announced an Agentic Identity Provider and Falcon Guardian, which discovers agents and controls that may run on Windows, macOS, and Linux endpoints.

Abdo argues that each vendor sees only part of the picture.

"If you're primarily an identity vendor or primarily a network vendor or primarily an endpoint vendor, that lens gives you some visibility to what agents are doing, but you need to have the other components as well," he says.

Microsoft's advantage, he adds, is that Entra, Defender, and Intune are already widely deployed and integrated, so customers aren't "having to string these things together from multiple vendors."

Microsoft says it will also take in signals from third-party security products. Partners can already publish agent risk events into Agent 365 through public APIs, Abdo says, though he could not yet name which partner integrations are public.

Forrester principal security and risk management analyst Andras Cser is skeptical.

"Most of Microsoft's integration with third-party players, especially in security, has not been first rate so far," Cser says. Because Microsoft has most of the products it needs in its own ecosystem, he adds, it is "interested in pushing its own products."

The question is whether that approach fits environments where agents run across AWS, Google Cloud, Salesforce, and ServiceNow. Last month, Okta announced the formation of the Blueprint Alliance with AWS, CrowdStrike, Google Cloud, Proofpoint, Salesforce, ServiceNow, and Zscaler to develop a shared architecture for securing agents across vendors.

Microsoft is not among the named members. Asked whether it would participate, Abdo said Entra has "always been built on open standards" and that "we're always exploring those things."

Okta, which formed the alliance, argues that no single vendor sees enough.

"No one company can secure agents alone," said CEO and co-founder Todd McKinnon in his keynote at Oktane, the company’s annual conference, last month.

Reacting to this week’s Project Perception launch, Harish Peri, Okta's senior vice president and general manager of AI security, says, "Microsoft's Guardian Agents feature will only be as good as the broader ecosystem it plugs into. If you want to catch intent drift in real time, you need signals pulling from your entire stack, not just one vendor's cloud."

Nevertheless, Peri echoes Nadella's framing. Because agents must be allowed to behave unpredictably to be useful, "we can't secure agents by trying to control how their models think," Peri says. "We need to control their authority."

The answer, Peri says, is "deeper interoperability and cross-vendor signal sharing built on open standards."

Cser interprets the Blueprint Alliance as "more of a partnership kind of map" than a true standard. Cser believes vendor-specific efforts like this alliance are "a marketing ploy" that tend to fade within a year or two. Enterprises need open standards any vendor can implement, he says.

Consequently, that leaves CISOs with an imperfect choice in what Cser calls "still a very fluid market." The current choices, he says, are either a Microsoft-centric approach built mainly on Microsoft products or a multivendor approach with "many vendors, many price lists," where integration "is almost always a suspicious kind of promise."

Some security vendors agree that treating agents as insiders extends the long-standing zero-trust and least-privilege principles rather than replacing them.

Denis Calderone, CTO of Suzu Labs, says the most malicious behavior may never look like an agent straying from its task.

"Dynamic permissions scope what an agent can touch, but the worst outcomes happen inside the authorized envelope," he says.

Calderone points to July's OpenAI incident as evidence that agents can work against the systems watching them. More than 1,000 agents in a cyber evaluation coordinated to game the system grading them, some by faking tool calls, before roughly 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face, according to METR.

Further, Calderone has concerns about Guardian Agents, noting that they are agents themselves.

"Securing agents with agents means the Guardian Agents themselves are overprivileged actors that can be manipulated or compromised," he says.

Cser shares Calderone's concerns about Guardian Agents. An unpredictable agent watched by another unpredictable agent creates "non-deterministic nature squared," Cser says. "Most organizations today are very careful about bringing guardian agents into the mix."

Following Perception's July launch, Forrester principal analyst Allie Mellen urged organizations to enforce "least privilege and least agency," limiting not just what agents can access but what they can do on their own. Microsoft meets the first test but not yet the second, Cser says.

"It is least privilege, but I wouldn't go as far as describing it as least agency," he says, adding that some specialist vendors are further along.

While Perception itself is in public preview, the new Guardian Agent capabilities are in use only inside Microsoft and with "a small set of select customers." They will be expanding to more external customers this week and to broader preview rings over the next few months. Microsoft plans to say more at its annual Ignite conference next month.

Project Perception builds on the controls in Microsoft 365 E7, the $99-per-user-per-month suite that includes E5, Agent 365, and Entra Suite, which supply the signals and enforcement points that Perception relies on. Microsoft hasn't disclosed whether the new capabilities are included in E7, but Project Perception is priced based on consumption.

Cser expects the release to push customers toward E7.

"I would almost be sure that this is another kind of making people buy stuff in more expensive packages that they don't currently need but may need in future," he says.

By his estimate, E7 comes to about $1,200 per user per year at list price, or roughly $600 after typical volume discounts of 40% to 50%, which "can be prohibitively expensive for a lot of organizations."

Meanwhile, Calderone says organizations don't have to wait. He recommends inventorying every agent, including those running on developer machines. Each should be assigned its own identity and credentials set to expire, and each should require human approval for consequential actions.

"That work is free today," he says, "and it's the foundation every one of these Microsoft controls assumes you already have."

Jai Vijayan contributed reporting to this article.

#9833. [$] LLM reviews for Debian's new queue spark debate

The Debian project has wrestled with the topic of LLM usage for years, which culminated in a general-resolution vote this August. The project voted in favor of the fifth, out of eight, option: "Responsible Use of Generative AI". With the door open to LLM use, the DFSG, Licensing & New Packages Team (usually shortened to "DFSG team"), which is relatively new, has started to employ LLMs in sending out reviews of packages entering Debian's new queue. The practice has raised a number of objections and questions about where lines should be drawn in the use of LLM-generated output.

#9832. Cyber Insurance's New Reality: Underwriting Isn't Enough

Rising AI, social engineering, and cloud risks are pushing carriers beyond risk transfer and deeper into cybersecurity itself.

The relentless evolution of the threat landscape has pushed cyber insurance companies to follow suit with a continuous expansion of cybersecurity posture requirements as well as taking an active hand in the defense process.

While cyber insurance has existed for years, the ransomware boom of the late 2010s and early 2020s transformed it from a niche risk transfer product into a central component of many organizations' security strategies. Today, policies cover everything from incident response and business interruption to legal costs and, in some cases, ransomware payments. Some of the names you'll see pop up around this space include Coalition, Chubb, AXA XL, Cowbell, and Resilience.

The threat landscape, especially when discussing enterprises, was never moving at a slow pace. But compared to the business email compromise and conventional ransomware attacks of five or 10 years ago, techniques are now evolving faster than ever, meaning insurance agencies must work harder to keep up.

Related:9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

Large language models (LLMs) have enabled threat actors to orchestrate complex attacks, streamline malware and exploit development, design phishing lures without typos, and operate at a scale never before possible. AI introduces uncertainty into threat models built largely around ransomware and data extortion attacks, which insurers have accumulated years of claims data around. Social engineering advancements could alter both attack frequency and severity faster than historical loss data can account for.

While outside of AI, attackers are also coming up with new social engineering tactics all the time, and cloud resource consolidation means compromised credentials or a single stolen API key can lead to devastating consequences.

Thomas Pytel, vice president at Cowbell, tells Dark Reading his firm believes in underwriting that continuously adapts to risk. "AI is changing the speed, scale, and credibility of phishing and impersonation, so historical loss experience alone is insufficient. Underwriting must assess how a business verifies identities, authorizes payments, and controls its own use of AI," he says.

According to a 2025 report from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC), cyber insurance premiums reached nearly $15 billion in 2024, up 7% year over year. Additionally, direct written premium (DWP) for the US market reached roughly $9.14 billion in 2024, compared with a market that was only a fraction of that size several years earlier. This underscores how cyber insurance has evolved to become a highly significant segment of the cyber-risk ecosystem.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

On the other hand, that same NAIC report cited nearly 50,000 claims across the US in 2024, the highest on record and a nearly 40% increase year over year. This could speak to the increasing number of customers choosing insurance, the aggressiveness of attackers, or both.

What remains to be seen is whether the industry's growth has outpaced its ability to accurately model the threat landscape.

Increasing insurance popularity also gave way to the rise of certain requirements for coverage, primarily demanding insurance customers uphold a certain quality of cybersecurity posture.

George Gerchow, IANS faculty and chief security officer at Bedrock Data, tells Dark Reading that a few years ago, these requirements were contained on a short form that "no one checked," but insurers now expect multifactor authentication (MFA), endpoint detection and response (EDR), immutable backups, and privileged access controls, while "some are moving to continuous telemetry instead of a once-a-year attestation."

Daniel Woods, head of emerging risks at Coalition, agrees. He says legacy underwriting models based on point-in-time questionnaires cannot keep pace, and this has been true since the ransomware epidemic took hold around 2020.

Related:Threat Modeling With 4 Simple Questions on a White Board

This occurred amid concerns that organizations would use cyber insurance as a replacement for patching, practicing defense in depth, or using strong data and authentication controls.

Better posture may be an objective net good no matter where it comes from, though it also risks turning security into a compliance exercise. Gerchow says these requirements can feel like that depending on who you ask.

"Insurance did more to get MFA and EDR deployed in the mid-market than any of us standing on a stage, and that part worked," he says. "But the application is a snapshot, and too many teams treat passing it as the goal. The carrier finds the gap for you at claim time. Lapsed MFA or an untested backup you attested to is now one of the fastest ways to get a claim denied."

Jeremiah Grossman, CEO of cyber loss prevention vendor Root Evidence, says insurance carriers are requiring more to be implemented, steadily, year over year, and "it seems to be working well for many." However, he says, "The issue is that organizations tend to not have the data to properly measure and model their risk, and their carriers are often in a better position to do so."

One relatively recent development in this space has been the rise of insurance organizations as active participants in the security process. While insurers these days broadly require MFA, security products like EDR, managed detection and response (MDR), and validated backups, insurance firms will also offer security products and services directly to their customers.

Coalition's offering includes access to an automated detection and response product, for example, while Resilience offers risk management tooling and Cowbell offers services including risk assessment, penetration testing, and training. All of these firms also work with other security vendors to recommend preapproved products and incident response services. While on the other end, traditional security vendors like Arctic Wolf offer products specifically for insurability.

Coalition argues its "Active Insurance" model has resulted in 73% fewer claims than the industry average and is why 56% of claims reported in 2024 were resolved with no out-of-pocket expense to those insured. Woods says that as the threat landscape intensifies, insurers that passively issue policies and hope claims do not exceed premiums will face increasingly worse results.

"The solution is for insurers to bring threat researchers and security experts in-house to monitor the threat landscape and actively support customers in improving protections during the life cycle of their policies," he says. "Risk transfer is still a fundamental component of cyber insurance, but so is ongoing protection and prevention."

Some risk remains difficult to model. Gerchow argues that if a crisis were to occur tomorrow where a major cloud or identity provider was taken down or compromised, the market would struggle to absorb it, and, he says, "the carriers know it."

"Look at where policy language is moving: war exclusions applied to nation-state activity with no declared conflict, widespread-event carve-outs, and small sublimits for dependent business interruption. CrowdStrike in 2024 was a bad update with no attacker anywhere in it, and it still grounded flights and stalled hospitals in a single morning," he says. "A real compromise of a major identity provider means every downstream customer needs forensics, counsel, and notification at the same time. If I'm a CISO this week, I'm reading the systemic-event exclusions in my policy first and assuming a big piece of that loss stays with me."

InfoQ Homepage News Vitest 5: Prioritises Performance with a Shared Vite Server, Trace View, and Stricter Test Defaults

Nov 03, 2026 2 min read

Vitest, the Vite-native testing framework maintained by VoidZero, has released Vitest 5.0, a major version that puts raw speed ahead of new surface area while quietly tightening several long-standing defaults.

Using a purpose-built benchmark suite that spans everything from a five-file utility package to a 1,280-module monolith, the team reports gains of roughly 8 to 25 percent across most setups, rising to 53 percent in VM pool scenarios. VoidZero summarised the release on X as "vm pools up to 53% faster, ~18% boost across the board including Browser Mode". The wins come from inline projects sharing a single Vite server, a stabilised on-disk fsModuleCache, fewer round trips between the main process and workers, and VM pools that reuse compiled code. A new vitest doctor command reruns a suite under alternative configurations and recommends faster options.

Browser Mode also gains a built-in Trace View that records each interaction and assertion as a DOM snapshot for step-by-step replay, while the new vi.when API lets a single spy return different values per argument.

clearMocks now defaults to true, unawaited async assertions fail rather than warn, hoisted vi.mock calls placed outside the top level now throw, and toThrow('') matches any error. As the independent OpenReplay breakdown puts it, most of these changes simply "break test code that was already wrong", but the dangerous ones are suites that pass locally on Vitest 4 and "go red in CI with an error that says nothing about why", usually call-count assertions that relied on mock history leaking between tests.

Vitest 5 requires Vite 6.4 and Node.js 22.12 or newer, and Yarn users must now install vite themselves because it became a peer dependency. The migration guide and v5.0.0 changelog document each change, and reporter output, attachments, and blob reports now live under one .vitest/ directory, so CI artifact paths need updating. Ecosystem catch-up is ongoing: Cloudflare's vitest-pool-workers issue notes its peer range pinned to v4 means any project pulling the new release "fails before a single test runs".

Against Jest, a recent head-to-head comparison scores Vitest ahead on performance and future-proofing yet behind on ecosystem and community, reflecting Jest's far larger install base and first-class React Native support. The advice to anyone considering the choice is unchanged, reach for Vitest on Vite, Nuxt, or greenfield projects, leave large working Jest suites in place, and let the two coexist in a monorepo.

Vitest is an open-source, Vite-powered test runner developed by VoidZero, the company founded by Vite creator Evan You that has joined Cloudflare. It reuses a project's existing Vite configuration to run unit, component, and browser tests with native ESM and TypeScript support, and is backed by more than 790 contributors.

Find the bugs your tests miss. Antithesis uses deterministic simulation to explore thousands of failure scenarios, uncovering hard-to-reproduce bugs before they reach production. See how it works.
